Benchmark. We develop a comprehensive industrial scene layout generation benchmark containing 40 descriptions of industrial scenes. These descriptions are written by 15 engineers based on their experience and split into 5 categories: geometric arrangement, focusing on geometric patterns; positional details, dealing with numerical measurements; object quantity, about the number of objects present; composite description, involving detailed, long-form textual descriptions; fuzzy description, an overview without precise specifications. The proportion of each category reflects its frequency of occurrence. Details are provided in Appendix A.9. Metric and evaluation. We adopt the pass@k metric (Chen et al., 2021), a commonly used metric for coding performance that measures the ratio of programming problems where at least one out of $k$ generated code samples qualifies. In the absence of automated testing tool suites, we rely on manual verification, carefully comparing each scene against its description. Our evaluation team consists of 3 members with expertise in industrial scenes and proficiency in the Process Simulate software. Due to the labor-intensive nature of the manual inspection, we sample 5 times for each description with temperature $t = 1$ and evaluate pass@1 with the estimator pass@ $k = \mathbb{E}[1 - \binom{n-c}{k} / \binom{n}{k}]$ , where $n$ is the number of samples for each problem (5 in this work), $c$ is the number of correct samples, and $k$ is set to 1. Each evaluator reviews at least one of the five samples of each description to minimize the influence of subjectivity, mitigating potential biases introduced by different evaluators. Models. Xiao Xia $^{1*}$ , Dan Zhang $^{1*}$ , Zibo Liao $^{2}$ , Zhenyu Hou $^{1}$ , Tianrui Sun $^{2}$ , Jing Li $^{2}$ , Ling Fu $^{2}$ , Yuxiao Dong $^{1}$

$^{1}$ Tsinghua University $^{2}$ Foundational Technologies, Siemens Ltd., China

# Abstract

The modeling of industrial scenes is essential for simulations in industrial manufacturing. While large language models (LLMs) have shown significant progress in generating general 3D scenes from textual descriptions, generating industrial scenes with LLMs poses a unique challenge due to their demand for precise measurements and positioning, requiring complex planning over spatial arrangement. To address this challenge, we introduce SceneGenAgent, an LLM-based agent for generating industrial scenes through C# code. SceneGenAgent ensures precise layout planning through a structured and calculable format, layout verification, and iterative refinement to meet the quantitative requirements of industrial scenarios. Experiment results demonstrate that LLMs powered by SceneGenAgent exceed their original performance, reaching up to $81.0\%$ success rate in real-world industrial scene generation tasks and effectively meeting most scene generation requirements. To further enhance accessibility, we construct SceneInstruct, a dataset designed for fine-tuning open-source LLMs to integrate into SceneGenAgent. Experiments show that fine-tuning open-source LLMs on SceneInstruct yields significant performance improvements, with Llama3.1-70B approaching the capabilities of GPT-4o. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/THUDM/SceneGenAgent.

# 1 Introduction

The advancement of large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020; Kaplan et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2023b; GLM et al., 2024) enables the automatic design of scene layouts, providing a promising direction for the automatic generation of industrial scenes. Automatically generated digital modeling of industrial

scenes can be used for design visualization, simulation, analysis, and optimization in manufacturing. Recent scene generation research (Sun et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024b; Hu et al., 2024) has made remarkable achievements in translating textual descriptions into 3D scenes, grasping a delicate understanding of spatial layout.

However, compared to general scene generation, the datasets and evaluations of which (Chang et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2023; De La Torre et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b) often prioritize qualitative plausibility, industrial scene generation presents the challenge of requiring quantitative measurements and precise positioning to maintain the functional integrity of machinery and safety compliance. # 2 Preliminary

Modeling Industrial Scenes. A scene can be represented as a collection of 3D models, denoted as objects $\mathcal{O}$ , drawn from an object library. Each object $o_i \in \mathcal{O}$ in the scene is characterized by its coordinates $c_i$ and direction $d_i$ . The coordinates specify the object's location on a two-dimensional plane, where the positive x-axis represents the front and the positive y-axis represents the left. The direction defines the object's angle rotated counterclockwise from the positive direction of the x-axis. The placement of an object, $p_i = (o_i, c_i, d_i)$ , encapsulates its spatial properties. The Euclidean

distance between two objects must be at least 1 meter to avoid collision. The set of all objects' placements $\mathcal{P} = \{p_i = (o_i, c_i, d_i) | o_i \in \mathcal{O}\}$ provides a modeling of the scene. Given an industrial scene's description, we aim to identify the objects and their placements to reconstruct the scene.

Code Representation of Industrial Scenes. We use C# code to leverage Tecnomatix APIs and model industrial scenes. The code aims to place objects from $\mathcal{O}$ according to the predefined placement $\mathcal{P}$ . We restrict the code's functionality to loading object models and placing objects to streamline API integration. The first selects and loads the model files of objects according to $\mathcal{O}$ , and the second sets coordinates and directions for objects with specifications outlined in $\mathcal{P}$ . The code is run in the Process Simulate software $^2$ to render the scene.

# 3 Method

This section consists of two parts: SceneGenAgent and SceneInstruct. Regarding the first part, we design an agent, SceneGenAgent, as shown in Figure 2, which leverages LLMs to translate the description into scene-modeling code. In the second part, we synthesize a new dataset SceneInstruct to fine-tune open-source LLMs to achieve performance comparable to API-based models.

# 3.1 SceneGenAgent

We introduce the workflow of an industrial scene-generating agent, which consists of two phases: Layout Analysis (Agent) aiming to extract and analyze the scene's layout and Code Generation for generating code using Tecnomatix APIs.

# 3.1.1 Layout Analysis (Agent)

SceneGenAgent performs layout analysis to recover the objects $\mathcal{O}$ and placements $\mathcal{P}$ . Layout analysis consists of three stages: object retrieval, layout extraction, and placement assignment.

Object retrieval. SceneGenAgent identifies the objects in the scene and retrieves the corresponding items from the object library. The agent executes all the following operations in a single LLM call using the description as input.

First, the agent generates a list of objects that should appear in the scene based on the description. This list includes ambiguously mentioned objects

like "a random object". The agent then maps the objects to their counterparts within the library by incorporating the objects from the library and objects found in the description into the LLM's input context and tasking the LLM to verify the presence of each object in the description within the library. If an object is not found in the library, the agent attempts to substitute it with a similar object from the library that conforms to the description. In cases where no suitable substitute is available, the agent removes the object. Consequently, the agent retrieves the object collection $\mathcal{O} = \{o_i\}$ from the library. Finally, the agent rewrites the description to reflect the retrieved objects' layout, replacing the original objects' names with those of the retrieved ones and retaining solely layout information. The output of this rewriting is the layout's concise depiction, denoted as the new description $s$ .

Layout extraction. SceneGenAgent extracts all layout information from $s$ . We categorize the existing layout information in $s$ into two types:

- Position, which refers to the positional state of an object, noted as $\mathfrak{p} = (o_i, l_i, d_i)$ , where $o_i$ denotes the object, $l_i$ the location, and $d_i$ the direction. Note that some objects may have no $\mathfrak{p}$ or their $l_i$ or $d_i$ may be missing because the description may not provide this information.

- Relation, which concerns the interactions between two objects, including aspects such as distance and relative direction. This is expressed as $\mathbf{r} = (o_i, o_j, r_{ij})$ , where $o_i$ and $o_j$ denotes the two objects and $r_{ij}$ their relationship.

The existing layout information in $s$ can be formalized into two sets $\mathbb{P} = \{\mathrm{p}\}$ and $\mathbb{R} = \{\mathrm{r}\}$ , representing the set of positions and relations respectively. The agent extracts all layout information with an LLM call, incorporating $s$ and $\mathcal{O}$ into the input and listing positions and relations in the output.

Placement assignment. SceneGenAgent assigns the final placement of every object $\mathcal{P}$ based on $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ and improves $\mathcal{P}$ through verification. Beyond adhering to the description, the assignment must also satisfy supplementary constraints, i.e., the specifications concerning object distance and orientation, to ensure the coherence of the scene.

Verification. The initial placement may contain flaws since the LLM may make common-sense errors or miscalcate values. Recent studies (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2024) have shown the ability of language models to critique their own decisions. Hence, SceneGenAgent iteratively checks $\mathcal{P}$ for the following potential errors: (1) whether the placement violates the constraints described in $s$ and (2) whether any objects collide, measured by the distances between adjacent objects. If errors are identified, the agent uses $\mathbb{P},\mathbb{R},\mathcal{P}$ , and the detected errors as input and attempts to fix the errors to generate a new $\mathcal{P}$ until no errors are found.

# 3.1.2 Code Generation

This phase involves writing C# code with Tecnomatix APIs to visualize the layout and model the scene. We design a code template containing basic code, such as initialization, and leave the parts responsible for model loading and object placement incomplete for the agent to fill. Following prior works (Zhou et al., 2023) that integrate code documentation into the model's input, we provide coding guidance alongside the template, aiding the agent in using APIs. The coding guidance includes usage guidelines and example code snippets corresponding to APIs. The agent employs an LLM to generate code, integrating $\mathcal{P}$ , code template, and

coding guidance into the input.

Potential errors can be identified within the generated code, including omitting code or making up methods or variables unsupported by Tecnomatix. The agent conducts a rule-based evaluation by scanning keywords associated with the APIs in the code to assess whether the LLM has correctly implemented the API calls. The detected invalid code is used as feedback to prompt the LLM to revise the code accordingly. Once the code passes the check, we run it to render the industrial scene.

When incorporated into SceneGenAgent, API-based LLMs handle all agent operations, and open-source LLMs are applied during placement assignment with Llama3.1-70B managing the remaining operations. # 4.2 Main Results Table 2 presents the performance of LLMs integrated into the agent. Larger models achieve high accuracy in the scene generation task, with GPT-4o exhibiting the highest pass@1 among all models, effectively solving most tasks. The open models' pass@1 generally remain lower than closed models. Smaller models solve only a limited subset of tasks, whereas Llama3.1-70B achieves performance comparable to closed models. The results also suggest that fine-tuning with SceneInstruct significantly benefits open models. After fine-tuning, all open models improve overall pass@1, with most models also exhibiting higher pass@1 in most categories. The performance drop in geometric arrangement and positional details marks the incidence of spatial errors rising, proving that the simplified settings lack the complexity required for precise scene generation.

To demonstrate the improvements achieved by powering GPT-4o with SceneGenAgent, we present several examples of scenes generated by GPT-4o, with and without the integration of SceneGenAgent, in Figure 3. In the examples, all scenes generated by GPT-4o with SceneGenAgent accurately reflect the descriptions, whereas those generated without SceneGenAgent exhibit various inaccuracies. Specifically, in the scenes generated without SceneGenAgent, the first example includes eight tables instead of the described four; the second misplaces the second table to the right of the first rather than behind it; and the third erroneously contains only one table instead of two and assumes the two robots are positioned relative to the same table rather than distinct ones. These examples highlight that even advanced models like GPT-4o can be susceptible to errors concerning the number of objects, their spatial orientations, and interobject relationships. In contrast, SceneGenAgent, providing a nuanced understanding of placement, contributes notably to complex scene generation ability, even improving the performance of GPT-4o, which already has strong capabilities.

# 4.3.2 Necessity of guidance in code generation

During the code generation phase, we provide the LLM with coding guidance related to Tecnomatix APIs. We assess whether the models require targeted guidance to utilize the APIs. We experiment by removing the API-specific instructions for object placement and instead instructing the LLMs to write Tecnomatix-based code to set the coordinates and directions of objects, drawing on their inherent knowledge regarding the Tecnomatix framework. This allows us to evaluate the models' performance without explicit coding guidance. We present this prompt for code generation in Appendix A.7.2.

We conduct these tests on GPT-4o and Llama3.1-70B without fine-tuning. All generated code fails to compile without API guidance, yielding 0 in pass@1 for both models. Rather than invoking the correct methods, the models often resort to fabricated methods not supported by Tecnomatix. This finding reveals that LLMs struggle to produce functional code without framework-specific instruction and validates our approach, emphasizing the necessity of API guidance for generating code.

# 5 Related Work

Generating scenes from textual descriptions has broad applicability across various fields such as indoor environments (Chang et al., 2017; Song et al., 2023), road traffic (Kar et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2021), and city planning (Lipp et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2024). A significant body of work focuses on generating structured 3D scenes by arranging modular and interactive objects with LLMs based on textual inputs. Unlike approaches that directly synthesize 3D representations such as radiance fields and point clouds (Bai et al., 2023; Cohen-Bar et al., 2023; Po and Wetzstein, 2024), these methods utilize pre-defined object assets, enabling the integration of generated scenes into downstream applications like programming in software. Studies using LLMs to generate 3D scenes introduce various techniques to control scene components. LayoutGPT (Feng et al., 2024), 3D-GPT (Sun et al., 2023), and SceneX (Zhou et al., 2024a) directly generate configurations of the scene, assuming that the LLMs are reliable for accurate arrangement. Other studies adjust the scene's spatial layout to better adhere to the text. LLMR (De La Torre et al., 2024) relies on validation to refine the LLM's layout planning. Some methods treat layout information in the description as constraints. SceneCraft (Hu et al., 2024) models these constraints using learnable scoring functions and optimizes these scores. Holodeck (Yang et al., 2024b) employs depth-first search on a relational constraint graph to find a placement satisfying the constraints. GALA3D (Zhou et al., 2024b) expresses the constraints with 3D Gaussian splatting representations to refine the layout. SceneGenAgent differentiates from them by regarding layout information as computable and refinable data structures, enabling precise placement through calculation and reasoning.

# 6 Conclusion

This paper introduces SceneGenAgent, an LLM-based agent that automates the precise generation of industrial scenes, translating descriptions into C# code using Tecnomatix API. We propose a layout analysis pipeline within SceneGenAgent that ensures accurate spatial positioning and compliance with complex numerical constraints in industrial layouts. SceneGenAgent uses a structured, calculable format to represent spatial specifications and infer overall layout planning through computation, iterative verification, and refinement. Furthermore, we fine-tune open-source LLMs with our constructed dataset SceneInstruct to improve their performance in SceneGenAg

Furthermore, we fine-tune open-source LLMs with our constructed dataset SceneInstruct to improve their performance in SceneGenAgent, approaching the capabilities of API-based models. We believe that SceneGenAgent can significantly enhance the efficiency and accuracy of industrial manufacturing and provide insights for further advancements in the scene generation field.

# Limitations

Broader applications. Our experiments predominantly focus on object assets and textual descriptions within industrial contexts. However, our proposed method for precise layout generation is not limited to such environments and holds potential for broader application in general scene generation tasks. Specifically, this method can enhance the quantitative accuracy of generated results across various domains. We plan to expand this work to more generalized scene generation by incorporating standardized benchmarks and robust evaluation methodologies in the future.

Evaluation methods. Due to the lack of automated tool suites for industrial software, our evaluation relies on manual evaluation, which is labor-intensive and inherently susceptible to subjective bias. Future work could explore developing automated evaluation methods to assess the generated scene's compliance with quantitative constraints, particularly in industrial software applications.

To facilitate a comparative analysis with SceneGenAgent, we select Holodeck (Yang et al., 2024b), a recently developed scene generation framework with publicly available source code. Specifically, we integrate Holodeck's placement planning module into the SceneGenAgent's framework by replacing the layout extraction and placement assignment components of SceneGenAgent with the corresponding modules from Holodeck. To evaluate performance, we compare the original SceneGenAgent and the modified version incorporating Holodeck's placement planning, employing Llama3.1-70B without fine-tuning as the backbone.

The pass@1 results for both variants are summarized in Table 4. The results indicate that the original SceneGenAgent substantially outperforms the version employing Holodeck's placement planning module. The substantial performance gap across all categories, particularly in geometric arrangement and positional details, highlights Holodeck's limitations in addressing the quantitative spatial constraints critical to industrial scene generation. - Quantity modification: Adjust the quantity of an object to a value between 3 and 10 if it is not assigned a placement or relations.

During each rewriting iteration, a rewriting method is selected probabilistically from a multinomial distribution. We collect the trajectories of SceneGenAgent using the constructed instruction dataset.
